question: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Although Article 174 TFEU explicitly recognises islands as areas with permanent natural or demographic handicaps, EU law still lacks a legally binding definition of ‘islands’ and ‘island regions’. Its absence is a barrier to the effective implementation of Article 174 TFEU. In this context, the future strategy should establish a systematic approach that integrates the island dimension into EU policies and redresses injustices against islands1. Island status must be enshrined as a horizontal parameter, integrated from the outset into the design of every European policy, legislative initiative and financial instrument through an operational model of ‘island-proofing by default’ in legislation and programmes. Taking into account that mandatory impact assessments for European initiatives affecting islands could be integrated into existing Better Regulation tools2: 1.

Will the Commission propose a legally binding definition of ‘islands’ and a typology of island regions on the basis of objective, multidimensional criteria3 and support their integration into the new MFF 2028-2034 for differentiated funding by island type?

How will the Commission ensure that the strategy produces a functional model of ‘island-proofing by default’ in European legislation and programmes, with the island dimension taken into account from the outset?

Does the Commission intend to introduce a mandatory ‘island clause’ in key sectors with significant territorial impact, through mandatory island impact assessments incorporated into tools such as territorial impact assessments?

The vast majority of island stakeholders who participated in the public consultation on the introduction of an ‘island clause’ into key policy areas, such as cohesion policy, transport, energy, digital infrastructure, CAP, fisheries, water/waste management and state aid. 2 Such assessments could be integrated into existing Better Regulation tools, such as territorial impact assessments. 3 The typology could be based on the OECD (2026) study ‘Policy Pathways Beyond the Shoreline: Enhancing Resilience and Innovation in Island Economies’, which introduces a hybrid territorial approach to classification based on multidimensional criteria, such as for example size, isolation, fragmentation, seasonality and dependence on external resources, and recommends functional typologies that capture the real interconnections of movement and services, especially for archipelagos like the Aegean. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The Commission adopted its first Islands Strategy1 on 10 June 2006, recognising the distinct characteristics of these territories. The Commission considers that existing legal and statistical frameworks already provide definitions and classifications that cover islands and are tailored to the objectives of the relevant policy areas. For example, Eurostat applies a statistical definition of island regions. The Commission will continue to assess whether existing definitions remain fit for purpose in their respective policy areas. Any future proposals would need to be considered in the context of the relevant sectoral legislation and impact assessments. The Commission applies an integrated approach to Better Regulation2 when preparing new initiatives. The Better Regulation Guidelines3 and Toolbox4 provide for the assessment of territorial impacts, including those affecting islands, where these are relevant and proportionate to the initiative concerned. Such analysis can help identify place-based risks, distributional effects and possible mitigation measures where impacts may affect islands differently from other territories. Under the new Multiannual Financial Framework (2028-2034) islands will continue to receive EU support. The Commission considers that territorial impacts affecting islands can be addressed through existing Better Regulation tools and procedures. In this context, it does not consider introducing further island specific mandatory impact assessments.
